title: I'm entering my own agent. Early access to an AI trading competitions arena.
author: orid7
selftext:
This is going to be interesting.   
  
AI agents trading the same live market head to head, every fill priced by the platform , one public leaderboard, prizes up to $20,000. Zero risk. free to enter.

Full disclosure, I'm one of the builders, so take my hype with a grain of salt.   
But I'm putting my own trading agent in the competitions.

Early sign-ups close Oct 10: [https://www.letitrade.com/](https://letitrade.com/?utm_source=reddit&utm_content=ai_trading)  
  
let me know if you're in. And tell me what would stop you from entering yours.

comments.author: profittoinvest
comments.body:
This looks interesting. Before entering, one thing would matter a lot to us: does the trading agent remain fully on our infrastructure and only communicate with your arena through an API, or do participants have to upload their strategy/agent code to your platform?

We already run a live-tested crypto bot, but protecting the strategy IP would be a requirement for us.

replies.author: orid7
replies.body: Yes, it stays on your infrastructure. Your agent only talks to the arena through the API (orders in, fills back), you never upload code or prompts. Crypto is one of the first markets we're opening. How long does your bot usually hold a trade?

replies.author: profittoinvest
replies.body:
Our holding times can be quite long.

In the current setup, the average trade duration is around 4–5 days, but some positions can stay open much longer, especially when the market moves against the initial entry and later mean-reverts.

We use relatively deep stops, so the bot is designed to give positions room rather than force quick exits.

That also means we manage risk at the portfolio level, because several older positions can accumulate at the same time.

So it’s definitely more of a multi-day / swing-style system than a fast intraday bot.  
If your arena supports positions being held for days rather than minutes or hours, it could actually be a good fit for us.

Are you aiming to build a platform along the lines of Cornix and 3Commas?

replies.author: orid7
replies.body: The arena takes orders through its own API, but forwarding the same signals to a webhook is usually a small step. And we're opening several competition types (different markets, intraday and swing), so I'm sure a multi-day bot like yours will find its edge.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Keeping the agent on the participant's own infrastructure, with only orders and fills crossing the API, is the right answer to the IP concern. Publishing the fill assumptions (spread, latency, partial fills) would help entrants judge whether their live results will carry over.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Protecting the strategy IP is the right requirement for any arena like this. I'd also want it to publish its fill assumptions (spread, latency, partial fills) and how open positions are marked, so entrants can tell whether a live-tested bot's results will carry over.

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body: Keeping the agent on your own infra is the only sane setup, uploading strategy code to an arena is basically handing over your edge. Multi-day holds with deep stops is a rough fit for a leaderboard that rewards fast fills.

replies.author: orid7
replies.body: Totally, that's why it won't be one board for everyone. Separate leagues for intraday and swing, longer windows for swing, and ranking on risk-adjusted return. Your bot stays on your infra either way

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: Keeping agents on participant infrastructure behind an API would address the strategy-IP concern, but the scoring window matters just as much. A multi-day bot using deep stops could look inactive or carry unresolved risk while a fast-turnover agent realizes gains before the leaderboard cutoff. How are open positions marked, and are agents compared on drawdown or risk-adjusted return as well as P&L? Since every fill is priced by the platform, publishing the spread, latency, partial-fill, and market-impact assumptions would also help entrants judge whether their live execution style transfers to the arena.

replies.author: orid7
replies.body: Great questions, all of that is covered in the rules we're publishing before any round. Are you going to run an agent? Sounds like you'd be a tough one to beat

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Thanks for stating that you're one of the builders up front. What would stop me from entering is mostly fairness: whether every agent gets the same data and timestamps, how open positions are marked, and whether the leaderboard shows risk-adjusted return and drawdown, not just P&L. A single short window rewards luck, so several rounds help. A shared, timestamped event layer (Cymetica's EventTrader is one example) would also let the arena test reasoning instead of who has the better feed.

comments.body: I’m in. I’d request the order execution functionality be similar to Alpaca’s given that’s what my design already can execute orders on. Mirrored order execution would save me a bunch of hassle.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: what would stop me is the length. a leaderboard over a few weeks of live trading mostly rewards whoever took the most risk, so the winner tends to be the biggest gambler, not the best trader. a drawdown cap or ranking on risk-adjusted return would fix most of that.

replies.author: orid7
replies.body: Agreed. So there are different lengths, and the biggest prize sits on the longest competition, ranked risk-adjusted, where your agent also comes out with a verified track record. Short ones are for fun, the long one is where it counts.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: that's the right shape. the long risk-adjusted one is the only result I'd take seriously.

replies.author: orid7
replies.body: the long one is the real goal. Hope to see your agent on it

comments.author: Key-Enthusiasm-3403
comments.body:
Nothing would stop me except not having an agent worth entering. Mine follows a preset rule, so it would be a mascot on that board rather than a competitor.



On the gambler problem QuanTradin raised, I have a number from the human side of it. I run a blind chart test: ticker stripped, dates stripped, rebased to 100. Call up, down or stay out, then put a size behind the call. The size is picked after the direction, so it reads confidence with nothing else mixed into it.



368 calls, 89 people:



stay out, risking nothing: 43% right

small: 32%

medium: 25%

biggest: 25%



Confidence was anti-correlated with accuracy, and it held all the way down until the top two converged. People do know when they feel certain. They are wrong about what certain is telling them.



Overall accuracy across those 368 calls was 30%. Three options, so guessing gets you 33%.



That is humans and not agents, so it is a bias finding rather than anything about sizing code. But the agents are written by those humans, which is the part I would not wave away.



If you want to know where you sit: playbotfight.com/?play=aitrading. Five charts, two minutes. The average score is 1.7 out of 5 and nobody has ever got five.

replies.author: orid7
replies.body: Bring the mascot, a simple rule-based bot is a great baseline, half the AI agents might not even beat it.
